jumbe-state-of-nkhotakota.t: A Swahili trading state on the western shore of Lake Malawi, a hub of the slave trade and of Islam in the region.
jumbe-state-of-nkhotakota.o: Around 1845 Salim bin Abdallah, a Swahili-Arab trader from the coast connected with Zanzibar, settled at Nkhotakota on the western shore of Lake Malawi. Taking the title Jumbe, he made himself ruler over the local Chewa and built the town into a trading base.
jumbe-state-of-nkhotakota.r: Successive Jumbes ran a commercial state that shipped ivory and enslaved people by dhow across the lake towards Kilwa and the coast; David Livingstone, who visited in 1863, described the trade. Mosques and Koranic schools made Nkhotakota a centre of Islam among the Chewa.
jumbe-state-of-nkhotakota.e: The Jumbe signed a treaty with Britain in 1889 and cooperated with Harry Johnston for a time, but in 1894 the British deposed the last Jumbe and absorbed Nkhotakota into the British Central Africa Protectorate.

juliana-republic.t: A short-lived republic in Santa Catarina proclaimed by the Ragamuffin rebels in 1839, famed for the exploits of Giuseppe and Anita Garibaldi.
juliana-republic.o: During the Ragamuffin War, forces of the Riograndense Republic under Davi Canabarro and Giuseppe Garibaldi advanced north into Santa Catarina, seeking a seaport. Garibaldi's boats were hauled overland to the coast, and in July 1839 the rebels captured the port of Laguna, where the Juliana Republic was proclaimed, named after the month.
juliana-republic.r: The republic was confederated with the Riograndense Republic and governed by local supporters under the protection of the rebel army. It had little time to establish institutions. In Laguna, Garibaldi met Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro, known as Anita, who joined him in battle.
juliana-republic.e: Imperial forces counter-attacked by land and sea, and in November 1839 they recaptured Laguna after a naval battle in which Garibaldi's flotilla was destroyed. The rebels withdrew to Rio Grande do Sul, and the republic ended after about four months.

judicate-of-logudoro.t: The northern Sardinian kingdom of Torres, one of four native judicates that ruled the island after Byzantine authority faded and a patron of Sardinia's finest Romanesque churches.
judicate-of-logudoro.o: As Byzantine control over Sardinia lapsed in the 10th and early 11th centuries, the island divided into four self-governing realms ruled by judges (judikes). Logudoro, also called Torres after the old Roman port of Porto Torres, covered the north-west. Its rulers held court at Ardara and appear in documents from the early 11th century.
judicate-of-logudoro.r: The judge ruled with an assembly of notables, the corona de logu, and governed through curatorie, rural districts. Land registers called condaghes were kept in Sardinian, among the earliest texts in the language. Judges invited Benedictine, Camaldolese and Vallombrosan monks, who built churches such as the Santissima Trinità di Saccargia, while Pisa and Genoa competed for its trade and favour.
judicate-of-logudoro.e: The last ruler, Adelasia, married Enzo, son of Emperor Frederick II, but died without heirs in 1259. The realm was then carved up between the Doria and Malaspina families, the Judicate of Arborea and the town of Sassari, which became the Republic of Sassari.

judicate-of-cagliari.t: Southern Sardinian kingdom ruled by native judges from Santa Igia until Pisa destroyed it in 1258.
judicate-of-cagliari.o: The Judicate of Cagliari, also called Calari, took shape in southern Sardinia in the 10th and 11th centuries as Byzantine authority lapsed. Its capital was Santa Igia, near the lagoon west of modern Cagliari, and its judges came from the Lacon-Gunale family, who alternated the names Torchitorio and Salusio.
judicate-of-cagliari.r: Its judges ruled the largest of the four Sardinian realms, granting land and churches to Italian and French monasteries such as Montecassino and Saint-Victor of Marseille. Pisa and Genoa competed for influence; in 1216 the Pisans built the fortress of Castel di Castro on the hill of Cagliari with Judge Benedetta's reluctant consent.
judicate-of-cagliari.e: When the last judge, William III, allied with Genoa, the Pisans and their Sardinian allies destroyed Santa Igia in 1258. The judicate was divided among Pisa, Arborea, Gallura and the Pisan della Gherardesca family. Castel di Castro grew into the city of Cagliari.

jarwanid-dynasty.t: A Shi'a dynasty that ruled Qatif and the Bahrain islands in the 14th and early 15th centuries under the shadow of Hormuz.
jarwanid-dynasty.o: The Jarwanids took control of Qatif and the Bahrain islands in the early 14th century, displacing the Usfurid dynasty there. They are usually described as an Arab family of eastern Arabia and adherents of Twelver Shi'ism.
jarwanid-dynasty.r: The dynasty governed the coastal towns and pearl fisheries and depended on the Kingdom of Ormus, to which it paid tribute and whose kings sometimes intervened in its affairs. The traveller Ibn Battuta, visiting Qatif around 1331, described a town of Arab tribesmen who were committed Shi'a. Twelver scholarship flourished in Bahrain under their rule.
jarwanid-dynasty.e: Around 1440 the Jabrid dynasty, Sunni Bedouin from al-Ahsa, conquered Qatif and the islands, ending Jarwanid rule.

judicate-of-arborea.t: Longest-lived of Sardinia's four judicates, centred on Oristano, whose Eleanor of Arborea issued the Carta de Logu law code in Sardinian.
judicate-of-arborea.o: Arborea emerged in west-central Sardinia, around the Gulf of Oristano, as one of the four judicates that replaced Byzantine rule in the 10th and 11th centuries. Its capital moved from Tharros to Oristano around 1070.
judicate-of-arborea.r: Arborea was a kingdom in all but name, ruled by judges with a council of notables. Barisone II was crowned King of Sardinia by Frederick Barbarossa in 1164. In the 14th century Mariano IV fought the Aragonese conquest, and his daughter Eleanor issued the Carta de Logu in 1392, a law code in Sardinian that remained in force across the island until 1827. Its economy rested on grain, herding and salt.
judicate-of-arborea.e: Arborea's army was defeated by the Aragonese at Sanluri in 1409. In 1420 William III of Narbonne, the last claimant, sold his remaining rights to the Crown of Aragon for 100,000 gold florins, and Arborea became the Marquisate of Oristano.

jabrid-dynasty.t: A Bedouin dynasty that ruled eastern Arabia and the Bahrain islands in the 15th century until the Portuguese arrived.
jabrid-dynasty.o: The Jabrids, from the Banu Amir branch of the Banu Uqayl, were a nomadic clan of Najd. Around 1440 they took al-Ahsa and then Qatif and the Bahrain islands from the Jarwanid dynasty, establishing a Sunni dynasty based in al-Ahsa.
jabrid-dynasty.r: Ajwad ibn Zamil, the greatest ruler, made his state the strongest in eastern Arabia, extended influence to Oman and made the pilgrimage with a large retinue, receiving honours from the Mamluk Sultanate. The Jabrids followed the Maliki school, sponsored scholars and controlled pearl fisheries and caravan routes. Their relations with the Kingdom of Ormus moved between alliance and rivalry over Bahrain.
jabrid-dynasty.e: In 1521 a Portuguese and Hormuzi force took Bahrain; the Jabrid ruler Muqrin ibn Zamil was mortally wounded, beginning Portuguese Bahrain. The dynasty kept al-Ahsa a few more years before fading, after which the Ottoman Empire took the region.

jamtland.t: Self-governing farming province of central Scandinavia, ruled by its own assembly on Frösön until King Sverre brought it under Norway in 1178.
jamtland.o: Jämtland, around the great lake Storsjön in central Scandinavia, was settled by farmers who, according to tradition, governed themselves without a king. The sagas describe settlers from both Norway and Sweden, and the region lay between the two kingdoms.
jamtland.r: The Jamtamót, the province's assembly, met on the island of Frösön and decided law and justice. The Frösö runestone, the northernmost Viking Age runestone in Sweden, records that Östman Gudfastsson had Jämtland Christianised in the 11th century. The economy rested on farming, cattle, hunting and the fur and iron trade.
jamtland.e: In 1178 King Sverre of Norway defeated the Jämts and made them pay tax, and Jämtland became part of the Kingdom of Norway, though it belonged to the Swedish archdiocese of Uppsala. It passed to Sweden by the Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645, and the Jamtamót tradition is still a point of regional pride.

juthungi.t: A Germanic people north of the Danube in Bavaria and Franconia who raided Roman Italy in the 3rd century and were later absorbed into the Alemanni.
juthungi.o: The Juthungi were probably a branch of the Semnones who settled north of the upper Danube after the fall of the Raetian Limes. They first appear around 260; an altar found at Augsburg in 1992 records a Roman victory over 'Semnones or Iouthungi' who were returning from Italy with thousands of captives.
juthungi.r: Their society was led by warrior elites capable of mounting long-range raids. In 270 they invaded Italy, and the historian Dexippus preserves a speech of their envoys to Emperor Aurelian claiming 40,000 horsemen. Aurelian defeated them, and Rome later recruited Juthungi as soldiers.
juthungi.e: Juthungi raided Raetia again in the 350s and 383, and Aetius fought them in 429 to 430, their last mention. They are generally thought to have merged with the Alemanni, whose Bavarian and Franconian neighbours inherited their land.

judicate-of-gallura.t: One of the four medieval kingdoms of Sardinia, in the island's north-east, ruled by native judges and later by the Visconti of Pisa.
judicate-of-gallura.o: As Byzantine control of Sardinia faded in the 9th and 10th centuries, the island divided into four self-governing realms, each ruled by a judge (iudex), who acted as a king. Gallura, in the north-east, emerged by the 11th century with its capital at Civita, near modern Olbia.
judicate-of-gallura.r: The judges ruled with an assembly of notables (corona de logu), drawing income from royal estates, herding and coastal trade. In the 12th and 13th centuries Gallura fell under the influence of Pisa, and through marriage it passed to the Pisan Visconti family. The last judge, Nino Visconti, appears as a friend of Dante in the Purgatorio.
judicate-of-gallura.e: Nino Visconti was expelled from Pisa in 1288, and the Pisan commune took over Gallura directly. The territory later passed to the Crown of Aragon after its conquest of Sardinia in the 14th century.

july-monarchy.t: The liberal 'bourgeois monarchy' of Louis-Philippe, King of the French, which rose from the barricades of 1830 and fell to those of 1848.
july-monarchy.o: The July Revolution of 1830 drove out Charles X of the Bourbon Restoration. Liberal deputies offered the throne to his cousin Louis-Philippe, Duke of Orléans, who took the title King of the French and accepted a revised Charter that lowered property qualifications and limited royal power.
july-monarchy.r: Government rested on a narrow electorate of wealthy men, and ministers such as François Guizot and Adolphe Thiers alternated in power. Railways, banking and industry grew, and the conquest of Algeria continued. The regime crushed republican and workers' risings, including the Lyon silk workers' revolts of 1831 and 1834. Guizot resisted all demands to widen the vote.
july-monarchy.e: An economic crisis and a banned campaign of political banquets led to revolution in Paris in February 1848. Louis-Philippe abdicated and fled to England, and the French Second Republic was proclaimed.

jin-dynasty-1115-1234.t: The empire of the Jurchen people, who overthrew the Khitan Liao, drove the Song from northern China and ruled it until the Mongol conquest.
jin-dynasty-1115-1234.o: Wanyan Aguda, chief of the Jurchen tribes of Manchuria, rebelled against the Liao dynasty in 1114 and proclaimed himself emperor of Great Jin ('Gold') in 1115, ruling from Huining. Allied with the Song Dynasty, the Jurchen destroyed Liao by 1125, then turned on Song, sacking Kaifeng in 1127 and carrying off two Song emperors.
jin-dynasty-1115-1234.r: The Jurchen kept their own military organisation, the meng'an mouke units, settling soldiers among Chinese farmers, while governing through Chinese-style ministries and examinations. A Jurchen script was created. Prince Hailing moved the capital to Zhongdu (Beijing) in 1153, and under Emperor Shizong the dynasty promoted Jurchen traditions while Confucian culture flourished. The 1141 treaty fixed the Song border on the Huai river.
jin-dynasty-1115-1234.e: Genghis Khan invaded in 1211; Zhongdu fell in 1215 and the court moved to Kaifeng. In 1234 Mongol and Southern Song armies took Caizhou, and the emperor Aizong killed himself. The Jurchen later re-emerged as the Manchus of the Later Jin (1616-1636).

jarrahids.t: Bedouin emirs of the Tayy tribe who dominated Palestine around Ramla and for a time challenged Fatimid rule by backing a rival caliph.
jarrahids.o: The Banu Jarrah, a leading clan of the Tayy, entered Palestine in the later 10th century as the Fatimids struggled to control Syria. Their chief Mufarrij ibn Daghfal alternated between serving and fighting the Fatimids and by the 980s held much of the country around Ramla.
jarrahids.r: The Jarrahids ruled as tribal emirs, collecting revenues and protection payments rather than building a state administration. In 1011-1013 Mufarrij proclaimed the sharif of Mecca, Abu'l-Futuh, as an anti-caliph in Ramla before making peace with Cairo. His son Hassan joined the Mirdasids and the Kalb in a 1024 alliance to partition Syria, but the Fatimids defeated it at al-Uqhuwana in 1029.
jarrahids.e: Driven from Palestine, Hassan and his followers took service with Byzantium. The family later regained influence among the Syrian Bedouin; Fadl ibn Rabi'a switched between Crusaders, Seljuks and Fatimids in the early 12th century, and his descendants led the Al Fadl tribe in Mamluk times.

jabal-druze-state.t: A French-created autonomous state for the Druze of the Hawran mountains, where the Great Syrian Revolt of 1925 began.
jabal-druze-state.o: In 1921 France reached an agreement with Druze leaders granting the mountainous Jabal al-Druze, south of Damascus, autonomy under French protection. Salim al-Atrash, of the leading Druze family, became its first governor.
jabal-druze-state.r: The state kept Druze customary leadership, with French advisers. After Salim's death in 1923, the French officer Gabriel Carbillet governed it, imposing roads and land reforms with forced labour and challenging the power of the Atrash chiefs. Druze anger led Sultan al-Atrash to rise in July 1925, defeating French columns and sparking the Great Syrian Revolt, which spread to Damascus before it was crushed in 1927.
jabal-druze-state.e: The state was renamed Jabal al-Arab, and under the 1936 Franco-Syrian treaty it was joined to the Syrian Republic, becoming the province of Suwayda.

javad-khanate.t: A small lowland khanate at the meeting of the Kura and Araxes rivers in central Azerbaijan, one of the least documented of the Caucasian khanates.
javad-khanate.o: After the death of Nader Shah in 1747, the governors of the district around the town of Javad, at the confluence of the Kura and Araxes, made themselves hereditary khans. The khanate covered the lowland steppe of Mughan and the river crossings that linked Shirvan, Karabakh and Persia.
javad-khanate.r: Its people lived from irrigated farming, livestock and fishing in the great rivers, and the crossings at Javad were an important route. Too weak to stand alone, the khanate was dominated by stronger neighbours, and from 1768 to 1789 it was a dependency of Fatali Khan of the Quba Khanate.
javad-khanate.e: As Russia advanced into the eastern Caucasus, the khanate submitted, and around 1805 the Russian Empire absorbed it. The town of Javad declined, and its lands were divided among neighbouring districts.

jingnan.t: The smallest of the Ten Kingdoms, a cluster of prefectures around Jiangling on the Yangtze that survived for four decades by bowing to every larger neighbour.
jingnan.o: Gao Jixing, a former slave adopted into a household close to Zhu Wen, was appointed military governor of Jingnan at Jiangling by the Later Liang in 907. After the Later Tang took power he was made Prince of Nanping in 924, and his family ruled the region as hereditary lords.
jingnan.r: With only three prefectures, Jingnan lived by diplomacy and commerce. It sat at a crossroads of Yangtze river trade, and its rulers accepted titles from the northern dynasties and from southern states such as Wu (Ten Kingdoms) and Later Shu at the same time. Other courts mocked them as 'Gao the Shameless' for seizing passing tribute and then apologising, but the policy kept the state alive.
jingnan.e: In 963 Song Dynasty troops, sent through Jingnan on a campaign in Hunan, occupied Jiangling, and Gao Jichong surrendered without fighting. His family was treated generously.

jin-five-dynasties.t: The Shatuo Turkic principality of Li Keyong and Li Cunxu at Taiyuan, the Later Liang's great rival, which conquered it and became the Later Tang.
jin-five-dynasties.o: Li Keyong, chief of the Shatuo Turks, helped the Tang drive Huang Chao out of Chang'an in 883 and was rewarded with the governorship of Hedong, centred on Taiyuan. He was made Prince of Jin in 895. When Zhu Wen ended the Tang and founded the Later Liang in 907, Li Keyong refused to submit.
jin-five-dynasties.r: Jin was a military state built on Shatuo and other cavalry. It continued to use the Tang reign title as a sign of loyalty to the old dynasty. Li Keyong's son Li Cunxu, succeeding in 908, defeated the Liang at Bochao in 911, annexed the Yan (Five Dynasties) of Liu Shouguang in 913 and won most of Hebei.
jin-five-dynasties.e: In 923 Li Cunxu proclaimed himself emperor of a restored Tang at Daming and within months captured Kaifeng, ending the Later Liang. Jin thus became the Later Tang.

junior-juz.t: The western division of the Kazakhs, whose khan Abulkhair first accepted Russian protection in 1731.
junior-juz.o: After Tauke Khan's death around 1718, the Kazakh Khanate split, with the Junior Juz holding the western steppe between the Aral Sea, the Caspian and the Ural River. Its tribes belonged to the Alimuly, Baiuly and Zhetiru groupings.
junior-juz.r: Under pressure from the Dzungars and the Kalmyk Khanate, Abulkhair Khan sought Russian protection, which was formalised in 1731. Russia built Orenburg in 1743 as a trading and military base on its border. The juz was nomadic, raiding and trading with Russia and Khiva. Syrym Datuly led a long revolt against both the khans and Russia from 1783.
junior-juz.e: Part of the Junior Juz formed the Bukey Horde in 1801. Russia abolished the khanship of the Junior Juz in 1824 and divided it into administrative districts, a process completed after the revolt of Isatay Taimanuly in the 1830s.

jarvamaa.t: Inland county at the heart of Estonia, conquered in the early 13th century and later a key holding of the Livonian Order.
jarvamaa.o: Järvamaa, Jerwia in Latin, occupied the central plateau of Estonia, bordering most of the other Estonian lands. Its central position made it a crossroads, and it appears often in Henry of Livonia's chronicle of the crusade.
jarvamaa.r: Järvamaa's elders joined the alliances of the Estonian counties against the crusaders and their Latvian allies. Its people farmed the limestone plateau and maintained hillforts as places of refuge. Its leaders accepted baptism after repeated raids around 1220.
jarvamaa.e: Fought over by Danes and the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, Järvamaa was assigned to the Livonian Order by the Treaty of Stensby in 1238. The Order built Weissenstein (Paide) castle there in 1265, and the region remained Order territory until the Livonian War.
